section.heading: Implicit Differentiation
section.paragraph: Fortunately, we don’t need to solve an equation for $$y$$ in terms of $$x$$ in order to find the derivative of $$y$$ . Instead we can use the method of implicit differentiation. This consists of differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to $$x$$ and then solving the resulting equation for $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ . In the examples and exercises of this section it is always assumed that the given equation determines $$y$$ implicitly as a differentiable function of $$x$$ so that the method of implicit differentiation can be applied.

section.paragraph: Note 1 The expression $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dx} = - x \slash y$$ in Solution 1 gives the derivative in terms of both $$x$$ and $$y$$ . It is correct no matter which function $$y$$ is determined by the given equation. For instance, for $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}$$ we have
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = - \frac{x}{y} = - \frac{x}{\sqrt{25 - x^{2}}}$$
whereas for $$y = g(x) = - \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}$$ we have
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = - \frac{x}{y} = - \frac{x}{- \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{25 - x^{2}}}$$

example.heading: Example 2

list.item: (b) Find the tangent to the folium of Descartes $$x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy$$ at the point $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ .
(c) At what point in the first quadrant is the tangent line horizontal?

example.paragraph: We can use either of the notations $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ or $$y^{\prime}$$ for the derivative of $$y$$ with respect to $$x$$ .

list.item: (a) Differentiating both sides of $$x^{3} + y^{3} = 6xy$$ with respect to $$x$$ , regarding $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ , and using the Chain Rule on the term $$y^{3}$$ and the Product Rule on the term $$6xy$$ , we get $$3x^{2} + 3y^{2}y^{\prime} = 6xy^{\prime} + 6y$$ or $$x^{2} + y^{2}y^{\prime} = 2xy^{\prime} + 2y$$ We now solve for $$y^{\prime}$$ : $$\begin{array}{rll} {y^{2}y^{\prime} - 2xy^{\prime}} & = & {2y - x^{2}} \\ {{({y^{2} - 2x})}y^{\prime}} & = & {2y - x^{2}} \\ y^{\prime} & = & \frac{2y - x^{2}}{y^{2} - 2x} \end{array}$$

(b) When $$x = y = 3$$ , $$y^{\prime} = \frac{2 \cdot 3 - 3^{2}}{3^{2} - 2 \cdot 3} = - 1$$ and a glance at Figure 4 confirms that this is a reasonable value for the slope at $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ . So an equation of the tangent to the folium at $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ is $$y - 3 = - 1\left( {x - 3} \right)$$ or $$x + y = 6$$ Figure 4 Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at the origin, then goes up and to the right until the point (3, 3) in the first quadrant. From point (3, 3), the curve then goes down and to the right, concave down so that it forms a loop in the first quadrant, reaches its leftmost point at the origin, and then goes down and to the right in the fourth quadrant, now concave up. A tangent line with a negative slope is drawn above the loop in the first quadrant such that the tangent touches the curve exactly once at the marked point (3, 3).

(c) The tangent line is horizontal if $$y^{\prime} = 0$$ . Using the expression for $$y^{\prime}$$ from part (a), we see that $$y^{\prime} = 0$$ when $$2y - x^{2} = 0$$ (provided that $$y^{2} - 2x \neq 0$$ ). Substituting $$y = \frac{1}{2}x^{2}$$ in the equation of the curve, we get $$x^{3} + \left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right)^{3} = 6x\left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right)$$ which simplifies to $$x^{6} = 16x^{3}$$ . Since $$x \neq 0$$ in the first quadrant, we have $$x^{3} = 16$$ . If $$x = 16^{1 \slash 3} = 2^{4 \slash 3}$$ , then $$y = \frac{1}{2}{(2^{8 \slash 3})} = 2^{5 \slash 3}$$ . Thus the tangent is horizontal at $$({2^{4 \slash 3},2^{5 \slash 3}})$$ , which is approximately $$(2.5198,3.1748)$$ . Looking at Figure 5, we see that our answer is reasonable.

note.title: Abel and Galois
note.heading: Abel and Galois
note.paragraph: The Norwegian mathematician Niels Abel proved in 1824 that no general formula in terms of radicals can be given for the solutions of the equation $$p(x) = 0$$ , where $$p$$ is a polynomial of degree $$5$$ with integer coefficients. Later the French mathematician Evariste Galois proved that it is impossible to find a general formula in terms of radicals for the solutions of an equation $$p(x) = 0$$ , where $$p$$ is a polynomial of degree $$n \geqslant 5$$ .
